Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "
hey, can you help me turn this into a prompt for reviewing our audio guide at the Larkhaven Museum? the exhibit is called Tides in Glass and covers the town’s working waterfront from 1900 to 1940. i need a review of the existing guide and practical revision recommendations, not a newly written full script. The audience is general museum visitors, including people who know nothing about local maritime history. The guide has six stops and currently takes about seven minutes and forty seconds to hear all the way through. We are not asking for an accessibility audit or a fact-check against outside sources; use only the information in this brief and identify anything you cannot resolve from it.

The six stops are, in order: a 1912 hand-blown harbor signal lamp; a glass plate negative showing three workers at the North Pier; a small sample of green bottle glass recovered from the shoreline; a 1924 map of ferry and freight routes; a 1936 photograph of the storm-damaged east breakwater; and an unsigned note from a dockworker describing a night shift. The lamp is the largest object, but the negative is the image most visitors stop to look at. The map is behind reflective glazing, and its smallest labels are difficult to read from the usual standing spot. The bottle-glass sample is in a low case. The storm photograph shows damage, but the collection record does not say how long repairs took. We have no confirmed name for the dockworker who wrote the note.

Here are some details about the intended visitor experience. A family group may listen together, but visitors also use the guide alone and at different speeds. People can skip a stop or start at any stop; the recordings do not lock visitors into a sequence. The gallery has a narrow doorway between stops three and four, and it can become crowded during school visits. A lift serves the upper gallery, but if the lift is out of service, visitors should be directed to the ground-floor information desk for an alternative route; don't say that the alternative route is guaranteed to include every object. We currently don't know whether the information desk has printed large-type maps on every day, so that should be treated as uncertain, not promised. The floor plan on the guide's landing page shows the six stops but doesn't mark quiet seating.

The current draft describes the signal lamp as “a voice of the harbor.” A visitor told us, “I thought the lamp actually made a sound, so I waited for it to light up.” Another visitor said, “I liked hearing how the ferry routes connected neighborhoods, but I couldn't tell which line on the map was for freight.” A teacher asked whether students could listen to just the storm story without hearing all the earlier stops. Those are comments, not proof that every visitor has the same experience. The guide's opening currently says, “Welcome to the harbor that never slept.” Our curator is concerned that the phrase sounds too sweeping because we don't have evidence about activity every night.

please have the eventual reviewer use these points as material, not assume missing history or visitor behavior:
1. The lamp is a signal lamp from 1912, and the label identifies it as hand-blown. We have not supplied evidence that it produced an audible signal, or that it was used every night.
2. The negative depicts three workers at the North Pier. Their names, job titles, and the date the photograph was taken are not known from the information here.
3. The green glass was recovered from the shoreline, but we have no supplied explanation for why it is green or how it got there.
4. The map is dated 1924 and shows ferry and freight routes. We do not have a transcription of the smallest labels or confirmation of which specific line a visitor meant.
5. The east breakwater photograph dates to 1936 and shows storm damage. The repair timeline is not in the collection record we have described.
6. The dockworker’s note is unsigned and describes a night shift. Don't assign the note to a named person or claim it is a first-hand account beyond what the description supports.

The review should consider sequence, clarity, visitor orientation, and whether the guide gives enough context to understand why each object is included. It should also consider whether the seven-minute-forty-second total and the ability to start anywhere are reflected in the proposed edits. We want recommendations that could be acted on by a small museum team, but no budget, recording software, staffing plan, or deadline has been provided. Please don't invent any of those. Don't assume the museum can move objects, alter cases, add staff, or change the building layout. It is fine to identify such matters as questions rather than prescribe them.

For the output, have the reviewer first provide a short assessment of what the supplied information does and does not establish. Then include a section called “Recommendations.” That section must contain exactly five numbered recommendations. In each numbered item, state the relevant evidence from this brief before giving the recommendation, so the reader can see what each suggestion rests on. The exactly-five-number rule applies to that Recommendations section only, not to headings or any questions that follow it. Finish with a short section of unresolved questions, only if the brief leaves questions that matter to a responsible revision. Do not write the revised audio-guide script itself.

one more thing for the ending: if the reviewer discusses the lift, retain the condition that it may be out of service and the specific direction to the ground-floor information desk, while keeping the availability of large-type maps uncertain and not promising that the alternate route reaches every object. Please keep the difference between facts, visitor comments, and unknowns clear throughout. The goal is a grounded review prompt that someone can use without having to ask me what the exhibit contains or what output shape i wanted.", "output": "Review the existing audio guide for the Larkhaven Museum’s exhibit, *Tides in Glass*, and provide practical revision recommendations. Do not write a revised audio-guide script.

## Exhibit and guide

The exhibit covers the town’s working waterfront from 1900 to 1940. It is intended for general museum visitors, including people with no background in local maritime history. The guide has six stops and takes about seven minutes and forty seconds to hear in full. Visitors may skip stops or start anywhere; recordings do not lock them into a sequence. Families may listen together, while other visitors listen alone and at different speeds.

The stops, in order, are:
1. A 1912 hand-blown harbor signal lamp.
2. A glass plate negative showing three workers at the North Pier.
3. A small sample of green bottle glass recovered from the shoreline.
4. A 1924 map of ferry and freight routes.
5. A 1936 photograph of the storm-damaged east breakwater.
6. An unsigned note from a dockworker describing a night shift.

The lamp is the largest object, but visitors most often stop to look at the negative. The map is behind reflective glazing, and its smallest labels are difficult to read from the usual standing spot. The bottle-glass sample is in a low case. The storm photograph shows damage, but the collection record does not say how long repairs took. The dockworker who wrote the note has not been identified.

## Gallery and visitor information

There is a narrow doorway between stops three and four, which can become crowded during school visits. A lift serves the upper gallery. If it is out of service, visitors should be directed to the ground-floor information desk for an alternative route. Do not say that the alternative route is guaranteed to include every object. It is uncertain whether the information desk has printed large-type maps every day, so do not promise their availability. The guide’s landing-page floor plan shows the six stops but does not mark quiet seating.

## Existing wording and visitor comments

The current draft describes the signal lamp as “a voice of the harbor.” One visitor said, “I thought the lamp actually made a sound, so I waited for it to light up.” Another said, “I liked hearing how the ferry routes connected neighborhoods, but I couldn't tell which line on the map was for freight.” A teacher asked whether students could listen to only the storm story without hearing all the earlier stops. These comments do not establish that all visitors have the same experience. The opening currently reads, “Welcome to the harbor that never slept.” The curator is concerned that this sounds too sweeping because there is no evidence about activity every night.

## Facts and limits

Use only the information in this brief. Do not assume missing history or visitor behavior, or fact-check against outside sources. Keep facts, visitor comments, and unknowns distinct. In particular:

1. The lamp is a hand-blown signal lamp from 1912. There is no supplied evidence that it made an audible signal or was used every night.
2. The negative depicts three workers at the North Pier. Their names, job titles, and the photograph’s date are not known from the information provided.
3. The green glass was recovered from the shoreline. No explanation is supplied for its color or how it got there.
4. The map is dated 1924 and shows ferry and freight routes. There is no transcription of its smallest labels or confirmation of which line the visitor meant.
5. The 1936 photograph shows storm damage to the east breakwater. The repair timeline is not in the described collection record.
6. The note is unsigned and describes a night shift. Do not assign it to a named person or claim it is a first-hand account beyond what its description supports.

## Review scope

Assess the guide’s sequence, clarity, visitor orientation, and whether it gives enough context to explain why each object is included. Consider whether proposed edits account for the total listening time of about seven minutes and forty seconds and for visitors starting at any stop. Make recommendations that a small museum team could act on, but do not invent a budget, recording software, staffing plan, or deadline. Do not assume the museum can move objects, alter cases, add staff, or change the building layout. Identify such matters as questions rather than prescribing them when appropriate.

## Required output

First provide a short assessment of what the supplied information does and does not establish.

Then provide a section titled **Recommendations** containing exactly five numbered recommendations. In each item, state the relevant evidence from this brief before giving the recommendation. The exactly-five-number rule applies only to this section, not to headings or questions that follow it.

Finish with a short section of unresolved questions, if questions that matter to a responsible revision remain. Do not write the revised audio-guide script.

If discussing the lift, retain the condition that it may be out of service and the direction to the ground-floor information desk. Keep the availability of large-type maps uncertain, and do not promise that the alternative route reaches every object. The review should be usable without further information about the exhibit or the requested output format."}]
